These chapters record visions and messages that God gave Daniel. They are recorded as apocalyptic writing. They were mysteries that confused Daniel. Daniel had explained dreams and mysteries to Babylonian kings. In the same way, Gabriel and other angels explained these mysteries to Daniel. Even then Daniel still didn’t understand the visions and messages completely.

The animals that Daniel saw were signs for governments. Hundreds of years later animals were also signs for governments in John’s visions. John’s visions were recorded in Revelation chapters 13, 16 and 19. The animals Daniel saw were signs for Babylonia, Persia, Greece, Egypt and Syria. The animals’ horns were signs for the leaders of those governments. The actions of those leaders were described in chapter 11. Some of these leaders were like the man of sin Paul described many years later.

The visions were about events after Daniel’s time. Some events described in these visions took place during the rule of Antiochus IV. He was a Greek king in Syria. He ruled over the Jews in the land of Judah and Israel. At one point he stopped them from worshipping God in the temple. This seemed like the end of the Jews being God’s people. That is one reason these visions are about a time called the time of the end. But the Jews firmly opposed Antiochus IV and won the victory over him. Jews recorded this story in books that aren’t included in the Old Testament.

Daniel’s visions bring hope and comfort. They remind God’s people that God will stop the evil actions of human rulers. God will take care of his people even when they face suffering. The angel Michael’s work made that clear. Michael helped God’s people in spiritual fights. Daniel read Jeremiah’s prophecy about the exile lasting for 70 years. Daniel recognised that the exile was God’s judgement against the people of the southern kingdom. He prayed and asked God to take action to end the exile. He trusted that God would have mercy on them. He believed this not because the Jews were godly and obeyed God. He believed it because God loved them. Daniel wanted all people to know that God is the one true God. He believed this would happen if God allowed Jerusalem and the temple to be rebuilt.

New Testament writers understood something about the visions and messages God gave Daniel. They understood that parts of them came true through Jesus’ life and work. This was the case with the son of man and the Eternal God. It was also the case with life that will never end. Jesus had this life when God raised him from the dead. His resurrection means that all who believe in Jesus will have eternal life.
T

The second half of the book contains visions given to Daniel. These visions assured Daniel and his people, both those in exile and those who had returned to Judea, that God controls the future. All empires will eventually fall before the kingdom of heaven. Daniel's people will be saved from their troubles ({{Daniel 12:1-3|Daniel 12:1–3}}), and God will resurrect and judge all people (see {{Daniel 12:13|12:13}}). Daniel interpreted these visions with help from divine messengers ({{Daniel 7:10|Daniel 7:10}}; {{Daniel 8:15|8:15}}; {{Daniel 9:22|9:22}}; {{Daniel 10:14|10:14}}; {{Daniel 12:7|12:7}}).
T

This final vision spans from 536 BC to a future when Daniel will rise from the dead and receive his inheritance. All earthly kingdoms will be destroyed. The eternal kingdom of the Son of Man will arise. God's people will finally be rescued, and death, the ultimate enemy, will be defeated.
T
*Darius the Mede*: See study note on Daniel 5:31. Darius's first year was likely 539 BC.
T

*Three more kings*: The Persian kings who followed Cyrus II were most likely: 

- Cambyses, who ruled from 530 to 522 BC,

- Gaumata, who ruled in 522 BC and was a usurper, and

- Darius I, who ruled from 521 to 486 BC.

The fourth was probably Xerxes I, who ruled from 486 to 465 BC (see study note on Esther 1:1). Xerxes was famous for his wealth, his army of 1,700,000 soldiers, and his large navy (see Herodotus, *Histories* 7.6). He used these forces to fight against Greece, but did not succeed. The Persians could not defeat Greece's growing power. God's guiding hand influenced the historical events in this chapter.
T

The messenger shared a broad overview of history. It started with Persia, continued through the fall of Greece, and covered the rise and fall of a wicked king or several kings ({{Daniel 11:21-45|Daniel 11:21–45}}). It concluded with the final resurrection and victory of God's people.
T

Alexander the Great was a powerful king (see study note on Daniel 8:21) who ruled from 336 to 323 BC. He conquered much of the known world in thirteen years, from Greece to India and from the north to Egypt in the south.
T

- Alexander died on June 10, 323 BC, in Babylon when he was 33 years old. He was at the height of his power and wanted to be worshiped as a god. 

- Alexander's descendants could not govern, and his brother Philip was not capable. 

- *because his kingdom will be … given to others*: Several of Alexander's generals divided his empire. By 301 BC, their conflicts had divided it into four parts (see {{Daniel 7:4-7|Daniel 7:4–7}}; {{Daniel 8:8-12|8:8–12}} and Daniel 7:7–7; 8:8–12). God guides history, and its end belongs to him.
T

The first king of the south was Ptolemy I Soter, who ruled from 323 to 285 BC. One of his officials, Seleucus I Nicator, took control of Syria and ruled from 321 to 281 BC. Both were military commanders under Alexander the Great. At first, the Ptolemies controlled Palestine from 320 to 198 BC.
T

In this passage, the *king of the South* refers to Alexander's general Ptolemy and his descendants, who ruled Egypt. The *king of the North* refers to Alexander's general Seleucus and his descendants, who ruled Syria and Mesopotamia. 

After Alexander's death, the kings of Egypt and Syria fought for control of Palestine, a strategically important land. The holy city and its people were caught between these two powers. These battles continued until their predetermined end ({{Daniel 11:27|Daniel 11:27}}, {{Daniel 11:35|35}}, {{Daniel 11:40|40}}, {{Daniel 11:45|45}}; {{Daniel 12:1|12:1}}, {{Daniel 12:7|7}}). 

Historical accounts of these events appear in *1, 2,* and *3 Maccabees* and in the works of Herodotus, Livy, Polybius, Porphyry, and Josephus.
T

Antiochus II Theos was the king of the north, who ruled from 261 to 246 BC. Ptolemy II Philadelphus was the king of the south, who ruled from 284 to 246 BC. They formed an alliance. In 250 BC, Antiochus married Ptolemy’s daughter, Berenice Syra, but abandoned her in 246 BC. Later, both she and Antiochus were murdered.
T

*one from her family line*: Berenice’s brother Ptolemy III Euergetes, became king of the south from 246 to 221 BC. He invaded Syria with his army, defeated the king of the north, Seleucus II Callinicus, who ruled from 246 to 226 BC, and occupied the fortress cities of Antioch and Seleucia. He expanded the Ptolemaic kingdom to its greatest size. When he returned to Egypt, he took their idols with him but left Seleucus II on the throne.
T
Seleucus II, the king of the north, attempted to invade Egypt in 242 BC but Ptolemy III defeated him.
T

- The sons of Seleucus II were: 

- Seleucus III Ceraunus, who ruled from 226 to 223 BC, and 

- Antiochus III the Great, who ruled from 223 to 187 BC. 

- *a great army … sweeping through like a flood*: Antiochus III aggressively tried to reclaim lost lands, including Palestine. 

- *as far as his fortress*: Antiochus III advanced to Raphia, near Egypt's border, in 217 BC. In the battle that followed, the king of the south, Ptolemy IV Philopater, who ruled from 221 to 203 BC, defeated Antiochus III and kept control of Palestine.
T

- Ptolemy IV’s success did not last long. In 198 BC, Antiochus III, the king of the north, returned. 

- Antiochus III had been conquering lands to the north and east. From these lands, he raised a fully equipped army that was much larger than before (compare *3 Maccabees* 1:1–5).
T

- A general uprising of Jews and rebel Egyptians who supported Antiochus III occurred. The king of the south was Ptolemy V Epiphanes, who ruled from 203 to 181 BC. 

- *they will fail*: The Egyptian commander, Scopas, stopped the rebellion in 200 BC.
T
In 198 BC at Paneas, King Antiochus III of the north defeated Egyptian General Scopas. He besieged and captured Sidon, a fortified city, and took control of Palestine.
T

*with destruction in his hand*: Antiochus III tried to make the Jews adopt Greek culture and abandon their ancient customs. However, some Jews welcomed him, and he responded by giving them special privileges. He allowed them to live according to their own laws. His son, Antiochus IV, did not treat them this way ({{Daniel 11:21-39|Daniel 11:21–39}}).
T

Antiochus III allied with Ptolemy V by giving his daughter, Cleopatra I, to him in marriage. Antiochus wanted to take over Egypt from within. However, his plan failed when Cleopatra became loyal to Egypt. Egypt then allied with Rome.
T

Antiochus III expanded his territory to include the coastlands of Anatolia, Macedonia, and Greece. However, the Romans defeated him in 191 and 190 BC. The prince was the well-known Roman general Scipio. He stopped the expansion of Antiochus III and forced him to give up the lands he had taken in the west and return in shame.
T
After this, Antiochus III stayed within his own fortresses. He was killed there in 187 BC by local people rebelling against him.
T

Antiochus III’s successor was his son Seleucus IV Philopater, who ruled from 187 to 175 BC. He was known for sending Heliodorus, a tax collector, to collect large sums of money. This money was needed to maintain royal splendor and pay the heavy tribute imposed by Rome. Heliodorus tried to steal from the temple in Jerusalem but was stopped by divine intervention (see *2 Maccabees* 3:1–40). Heliodorus murdered Seleucus after a short seven-year reign.
T

Antiochus IV Epiphanes came to power next, ruling from 175 to 163 BC. He is the *small horn* mentioned in {{Daniel 8:9-14|Daniel 8:9–14}}, {{Daniel 8:23-26|23–26}}. His story is vividly described in *1 Maccabees* 1:7–6:16; *2 Maccabees* 1:1–10:5; *4 Maccabees* 4:15–18:5. Antiochus was considered despicable because he seized the throne and for his actions as king. He was not in line for royal succession and took the throne from his brother’s son.
T

The *prince of the covenant* was Onias III, the high priest (see study notes on Daniel 9:25–26). Antiochus IV removed him in 175 BC and replaced him with his brother Jason (*2 Maccabees* 4:7–10). In 171 BC, Menelaus murdered Onias and became high priest from 171 to 162 BC. Menelaus supported Antiochus IV’s plan to spread Greek culture (see study note on Daniel 9:27).
T
*he will act deceitfully*: Antiochus IV made false promises to introduce Greek religion into Judea. Lawless followers supported his policies (see *1 Maccabees* 1:11–15).
T
*the richest provinces*: Antiochus IV took the temple's riches, demanded large payments from Jerusalem, and placed troops there (*1 Maccabees* 1:29–40).
T
Ptolemy VI Philometor ruled from 181 to 146 BC. He was the *king of the South*. Antiochus IV attacked Egypt twice between 170 and 168 BC (1 Maccabees 1:17–19).
T

In 170 BC, Antiochus IV attacked Jerusalem and the temple. He killed thousands and enslaved many others (*1 Maccabees* 1:20–42; *2 Maccabees* 5:1–23). His arrogance was great (*1 Maccabees* 1:24–25; compare {{Daniel 7:28|Daniel 7:28}}; {{Daniel 8:9|8:9}}).
T

- Antiochus IV invaded the south (Egypt) again (see Polybius, *Histories* 29.1). 

- The warships from western coastlands refer to the Romans. The Roman general Popilius Laenas drew a circle in the sand, made Antiochus stand inside it, and forced him to decide whether to return home or prepare for war with Rome before leaving the circle. 

Fearing the Roman fleet, Antiochus chose to withdraw and return home. He then took out his anger and humiliation on the Jews, the people of the holy covenant. He captured Jerusalem in 167 BC and rewarded those who joined him. He defiled the altar (see {{Daniel 8:9-14|Daniel 8:9–14}}, {{Daniel 8:23-26|23–26}}), stopped the sacrifices, set up a statue of the Greek god Zeus in the temple, and persecuted and killed those who refused to abandon the covenant (see *1 Maccabees* 1:62–64; compare {{Daniel 9:27|Daniel 9:27}}; {{Matthew 24:15|Matthew 24:15}}).
T
*the abomination of desolation*: See study note on Daniel 9:27.
T

Wise people know God and his laws and follow them, even in a hostile and deceptive environment. Many were killed for their faithfulness to God and his laws during this time (*1 Maccabees* 1:11; {{Daniel 7:19|Daniel 7:19}}; *2 Maccabees* 6–7).
T

Help arrived when Mattathias's family and their supporters (the Maccabees) started a national revolt. Antiochus was busy elsewhere and could not stop it. In 164 BC, three years after the temple was desecrated, the Maccabees recaptured Jerusalem. They removed the statue of Zeus, cleansed the altar, and restored daily sacrifices ({{Daniel 8:11-14|Daniel 8:11–14}}, {{Daniel 8:26|26}}; *1 Maccabees* 1:59). This event is celebrated during *Hanukkah* (see {{John 10:22|John 10:22}}).
T

- Antiochus IV considered himself equal to God (*2 Maccabees* 9:1–10:12), but God restrained him until the time of wrath ended. 

- *what has been decreed must be accomplished*: Antiochus suddenly developed a painful disease and died in 163 BC in the mountains of Persia (see {{Daniel 8:25|Daniel 8:25}}; *1 Maccabees* 4:52–53; 6:16; *2 Maccabees* 9:4, 28; 10:5).
T
Some interpreters see these verses as a transition from the earthly Antiochus IV to a figure who is larger than history itself ({{Daniel 7:8|Daniel 7:8}}).
T

- *no regard for the gods of his father*: He abandoned the Syrian gods to worship Greek gods. 

- The *one desired by women* might be a Canaanite or Egyptian fertility deity. 

- History does not mention a god of fortresses, but this might refer to the lavish gifts Antiochus gave to cities and Greek temples. He might have done this to improve his reputation and power (see Livy, *History* 41.20).
T
No known southern or northern king did these actions.
T

Most commentators believe these verses describe the end of history (compare {{Mark 13:14|Mark 13:14}}; {{2 Thessalonians 2:3-12|2 Thessalonians 2:3–12}}; {{Revelation 19:19-21|Revelation 19:19–21}}). These verses reflect the actions of Antiochus IV, but there is no historical record of these events. Antiochus serves as a model for future rulers who oppose the God of gods.
T

- *the Beautiful Land*: Israel (compare {{Daniel 8:9|Daniel 8:9}}; {{Daniel 11:16|11:16}}) is once more the target of an evil king's attack. 

- Moab, Edom, and Ammon were nations that surrounded ancient Israel and Judah.
T

- The holy mountain includes Zion, Jerusalem, and the temple, where God chose for his name to dwell.

- The sea likely refers to the Mediterranean Sea.
T

- Michael was the angel who protected Israel (see {{Daniel 10:13|Daniel 10:13}}, {{Daniel 10:21|21}}; {{Revelation 2:1|Revelation 2:1}}, {{Revelation 2:8|8}}, {{Revelation 2:12|12}}). 

- *the book*: This might be the Book of Truth ({{Daniel 10:21|Daniel 10:21}}; see {{Daniel 7:10|7:10}}). 

- *will be delivered*: All past rescues of God's people in Daniel (for example, {{Daniel 3:28|Daniel 3:28}}; {{Daniel 6:27|6:27}}) hinted at and now lead to the resurrection from the dead ({{Daniel 12:2-3|12:2–3}}).
T
In the end times, God will save his people and defeat all enemies, including death.
T
Everlasting life is entirely free from shame or disgrace (compare {{Genesis 2:25|Genesis 2:25}}; {{Genesis 3:7|3:7}}).
T

- Wise people know their God (compare {{Daniel 1:4|Daniel 1:4}}, {{Daniel 1:17|17}}; {{Daniel 8:25|8:25}}; {{Daniel 9:22|9:22}}, {{Daniel 9:25|25}}; {{Daniel 11:32-35|11:32–35}}; {{Daniel 12:10|12:10}}). 

- To shine is a common metaphor for life, purity, righteousness, and glory.
T
Daniel had to keep the prophecy a secret (compare {{Daniel 7:28|Daniel 7:28}}; {{Daniel 8:26|8:26}}). God would reveal it at the right time, at the end.
T

- The river was the Tigris River ({{Daniel 10:4|Daniel 10:4}}). 

- Two others confirmed God's promises (see {{Numbers 35:30|Numbers 35:30}}; {{Deuteronomy 19:15|Deuteronomy 19:15}}).
T

- *a time, and times, and half a time*: God sets times for everything as he controls earthly and heavenly events (see study note on Daniel 7:24–25). 

- The breaking of the holy people was part of God's plan to purify them ({{Daniel 12:10|Daniel 12:10}}).
T

- God did not reveal exactly how and when everything would end. Daniel would not witness the end ({{Daniel 12:13|Daniel 12:13}}); his task was to live his life with faith. 

- *purified, made spotless, and refined*: God would use violent and terrifying times to improve the moral and religious character of his people (compare {{Daniel 11:35|Daniel 11:35}}). 

- Being wise means understanding God's ways and living by them. The wicked will not understand or change their ways, even if someone explains the vision to them.
T

- *the abomination of desolation*: See {{Daniel 8:13-14|Daniel 8:13–14}}, {{Daniel 8:23-26|23–26}}; {{Daniel 11:29-35|11:29–35}}. See also study note on Daniel 9:27. 

- God's people must wait and stay faithful when the end times come. 

- *1,290 days … 1,335 days*: Some interpreters think these numbers relate to events during the reign of Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Others believe they are symbolic. 

The number 1,290 equals 43 lunar months of 30 days each, which is about three and a half years in the solar calendar. This might represent the final half of the last “set of seven” ({{Daniel 9:27|Daniel 9:27}}). 

The number 1,335 might mean an extra 45 days of waiting until the end. Those who endure the entire time, and then some, will see God act for his people.
T
Daniel died before the end times, but he knew he would rise again. The end times refer to when even the dead rise ({{Daniel 12:1-3|Daniel 12:1–3}}) and God's everlasting kingdom is established.
